explanation:
# How the Selic Rate Affects Your Savings

The **Selic rate** (*Sistema Especial de Liquidação e de Custódia*) is Brazil's benchmark interest rate, set by the **COPOM** (*Comitê de Política Monetária*) of the **Banco Central do Brasil** at meetings held roughly every 45 days — eight times per year. It serves as the floor for the cost of money in reais and the base yield for government bonds (*Tesouro Selic*), CDI-linked CDBs, LCIs, LCAs, and fixed-income funds. When COPOM raises the Selic to fight inflation, returns on fixed income rise; when it cuts to stimulate the economy, those returns fall.

> **Current context:** After peaking at 13.75% between August 2022 and August 2023, the Selic began a cutting cycle. As of early 2025 it stands at **13.25%**, following COPOM's decision in January 2025 to resume hikes in response to persistent inflation pressure. Always check the [Banco Central do Brasil website](https://www.bcb.gov.br) for the official current rate before making any financial decision.

---

## How It's Calculated

This calculator compounds your initial amount at the Selic rate over the chosen term. It first converts the annual Selic to an equivalent monthly rate, then compounds month by month:

```
monthlyRate  = (1 + Selic/100)^(1/12) − 1
finalBalance = amount × (1 + monthlyRate)^months
return       = finalBalance − amount
```

It also displays **simple interest** for reference:

```
simpleReturn = amount × (Selic/100) × (months/12)
```

At exactly 12 months, both methods produce the same result. Over longer terms, compound interest yields more because each month's interest itself earns interest in subsequent months — the longer the horizon, the larger this gap.

---

## How the Selic Affects Your Gross Return

| Annual Selic | Final balance (R$ 10,000, 12 mo) | Gross return |
|---|---|---|
| 9.00% | R$ 10,900.00 | R$ 900.00 |
| 10.50% | R$ 11,050.00 | R$ 1,050.00 |
| 12.00% | R$ 11,200.00 | R$ 1,200.00 |
| 13.25% | R$ 11,325.00 | R$ 1,325.00 |
| 13.75% | R$ 11,375.00 | R$ 1,375.00 |

*Values use simple annual compounding for illustration. The calculator uses exact monthly compounding, which produces marginally higher results.*

---

## Selic vs CDI: What's the Difference?

The **CDI** (*Certificado de Depósito Interbancário*) is the rate at which banks lend overnight to each other. It tracks the Selic extremely closely — historically around **0.10 percentage points below** it. This is why a CDB advertised as "100% of the CDI" yields almost exactly the Selic rate. For a quick estimate, using the Selic here is entirely valid.

---

## Gross vs Net Return: The Taxes You Cannot Ignore

This calculator shows **gross returns**. In Brazil, fixed-income investments are subject to **withholding income tax (IR)** on gains, following a regressive table:

Additionally, investments held for **up to 30 days** are subject to **IOF** (*Imposto sobre Operações Financeiras*), which is charged on a regressive daily scale from 96% (day 1) down to 0% (day 30). For any investment you plan to hold less than a month, IOF will significantly erode your return.

**Important exception:** *LCI* (Letra de Crédito Imobiliário) and *LCA* (Letra de Crédito do Agronegócio) are **exempt from IR for individuals**, which can make a CDB at 100% CDI less attractive than an LCI at 88% CDI when tax is applied.

---

## What This Calculator Does NOT Include

- **Inflation (IPCA):** The Selic is a nominal rate. To know your real purchasing-power gain, subtract inflation. If the Selic is 13.25% and IPCA runs at 5%, your real return is roughly 7.8% — not 13.25%.
- **Income tax and IOF:** As detailed above. Always calculate net-of-tax return before comparing products.
- **Fund fees (taxa de administração):** Fixed-income funds charge annual management fees, typically 0.2%–1.5%, which directly reduce your effective yield.
- **Payout structures:** *Tesouro Selic* pays semiannual interest coupons on some series; this calculator assumes full reinvestment.

---

## Common Mistakes

1. **Confusing gross and net return.** A CDB at 13% Selic held for 6 months yields roughly 10.1% net after 22.5% IR — not 13%.
2. **Assuming the Selic stays constant.** COPOM meets eight times per year. For multi-year projections, using today's rate as fixed overstates or understates results significantly.
3. **Ignoring the CDI spread.** "110% of the CDI" sounds high, but at a 13.25% Selic, 110% CDI ≈ 14.5% gross — meaningful only if you also account for tax and holding period.
4. **Forgetting FGC coverage.** CDBs, LCIs, and LCAs are guaranteed by the *Fundo Garantidor de Créditos* (FGC) up to **R$ 250,000 per institution, per CPF** (aggregate limit of R$ 1 million per 4-year period). *Tesouro Selic* has no such cap — it is backed directly by the federal government.

faq.q: What is the Selic rate and who sets it?
faq.a: The Selic is Brazil's benchmark interest rate. It is set by the COPOM (Comitê de Política Monetária) of the Banco Central do Brasil at meetings held roughly every 45 days. It is the reference rate for government bonds and, in practice, the base yield for all fixed income denominated in reais.

The COPOM (Comitê de Política Monetária) is the body of the Banco Central do Brasil that decides the level of the Selic rate. It meets eight times a year and its decisions set the cost of money in reais and the yield on fixed-income investments.

faq.q: How does a Selic increase affect my savings?
faq.a: When the COPOM raises the Selic, the yield on Selic-linked investments (Tesouro Selic, CDBs at 100% of the CDI, DI funds) rises almost immediately for new and post-fixed investments. A Selic cut lowers that yield. This calculator shows the concrete effect in reais.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Selic and the CDI?
faq.a: The Selic is the central bank's reference rate; the CDI is the rate for interbank loans. The CDI tracks the Selic closely, usually about 0.10 points below it, so a CDB paying 100% of the CDI yields almost the same as the Selic. Using the Selic here is a good approximation.

faq.q: Is the result gross or net of taxes?
faq.a: It is gross, before income tax (IR). In Brazil, fixed income pays a regressive IR on the return: 22.5% up to 180 days, 20% from 181 to 360 days, 17.5% from 361 to 720 days, and 15% beyond 720 days. IR is charged only on the gain, not on the principal.

faq.q: Why do you show both simple and compound interest?
faq.a: Compound interest is the real case for Brazilian fixed income: interest is reinvested and earns more interest. Simple interest is a linear reference that is easy to understand. At 12 months both coincide; over longer terms compound yields more. We show both so you can see the difference.

faq.q: Does this calculator work for the poupança?
faq.a: Not directly. The poupança (traditional savings account) does not pay the full Selic: it pays 70% of the Selic plus the TR when the Selic is 8.5% per year or below, or 0.5% per month plus TR when it is higher. This calculator estimates the return at the full Selic, closer to a Tesouro Selic bond or a CDB at 100% of the CDI.

faq.q: What Selic rate should I use if I don't know it?
faq.a: In 2026 the Selic is around 9% to 12% per year, but it is worth checking the current value because the COPOM adjusts it every 45 days. The official figure is published on the Banco Central do Brasil website. For CDB investments you can use the current CDI, which is almost identical to the Selic.

faq.q: Can I calculate monthly contributions with this tool?
faq.a: No, this calculator assumes a single initial deposit that compounds at the Selic over the term. For periodic contributions (a fixed amount each month) you need a recurring-contribution calculator that adds the return of each deposit based on how long it stayed invested.
